methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a preplanned subgroup analysis of a 29-institution retrospective multicenter observational cohort (REVEAL/WJOG15421L), with 229 post-operative recurrence cases analyzed. Strengths include use of univariate/multivariate logistic regression with backward stepwise selection to identify predictors of multigene testing, and Kaplan-Meier/HR comparisons for OS. Weaknesses: no a priori power calculation for the subgroup analysis; no multiplicity adjustment across many testing comparisons (biomarkers, subgroups, four survival contrasts); timing of biomarker testing (pre- vs post-recurrence) is a known confounder that is acknowledged but not addressed analytically (e.g., sensitivity analysis excluding pre-recurrence testing). OS is defined from surgery to death, which risks immortal-time/lead-time bias when comparing post-operative recurrence against primary advanced disease and is not adjusted via landmark or stage-matched analysis. Selection bias from non-consecutive enrollment at specialized centers is acknowledged but not quantified.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Design is a retrospective, multicenter observational cohort study (preplanned subgroup) corresponding to Oxford CEBM level 2b. The question (real-world implementation of multigene testing in post-operative NSCLC recurrence) is clinically relevant for perioperative personalized medicine and is linked to patient-relevant OS and an operational quality endpoint (testing rate). It identifies actionable implementation gaps (nonadenocarcinoma histology, >3 years from surgery) that could inform quality-improvement and biomarker workflows, but it does not alter standard of care. Generalizability is limited to specialized Japanese cancer centers using Oncomine DxTT, so translational impact is plausible but indirect.

reporting_quality.justification: The authors explicitly state they followed STROBE and the study is registered (UMIN000046079). Eligibility, enrollment flow (Supplementary Figure S1), variable definitions, OS definition, and statistical methods are generally reported, with Table 1 providing baseline characteristics. Gaps versus STROBE include limited reporting of handling of missing data (e.g., unknown ECOG, smoking), no explicit confounders considered a priori for the OS comparison, no formal sensitivity analyses, and incomplete reporting of how patients contributing testing before recurrence were handled. Data/code availability is weak: no deposited dataset, no code repository, and software versions listed (Python/pandas/lifelines) are not accompanied by an analytic code release; the data availability section was redacted but no deposition identifier is visible.

novelty_literature.justification: The authors claim this is the first study to specifically examine biomarker/multigene testing status and prognosis in post-operative recurrent NSCLC, which is a credible gap-filling claim within the real-world Japanese context and the Oncomine DxTT era. Novelty is empirical and population-focused (post-op recurrence subgroup) rather than conceptual or methodological; the parent REVEAL cohort has already reported overall biomarker testing patterns (Sakamoto 2023), and prior work has shown prognostic advantage of post-op recurrence versus de novo advanced disease. The identification of >3-year interval and nonadenocarcinoma histology as independent predictors of non-submission is a meaningful but incremental extension of known barriers to NGS adoption.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with a clear IMRaD structure, defined acronyms on first use, and an abstract that quantitatively and faithfully reflects the main findings. Figure and table captions are informative and standalone-interpretable, and the Discussion integrates results with guidelines and perioperative targeted-therapy context (IMpower010, ADAURA, CheckMate 816). Minor issues: Table 1 and Table 2 inline text in this blinded render are dense and would benefit from clearer layout; some redundancy exists between the bulleted highlights and abstract; a few places could tighten mechanistic speculation. Overall it reads as publication-ready scientific prose.

key_strengths: Multicenter (29 institutions) real-world cohort with a preplanned subgroup analysis of 229 post-operative recurrence cases addressing a documented gap in multigene testing implementation
Clinically actionable findings: nonadenocarcinoma histology and >3-year surgery-to-recurrence interval independently predict non-submission for multigene testing (OR 0.40 and 0.43, respectively)
STROBE-aligned reporting with trial registration (UMIN000046079), explicit eligibility flow, and transparent description of testing success rates by specimen type
Clear writing, informative tables/figure captions, and discussion that situates findings within current perioperative personalized medicine (IMpower010, ADAURA, CheckMate 816)
key_concerns: OS defined from surgery introduces immortal-time/lead-time bias when comparing post-operative recurrence to primary advanced disease; no landmark or stage-adjusted sensitivity analysis
No multiplicity correction across numerous biomarker/subgroup/survival comparisons and no a priori power calculation for the subgroup
Timing of biomarker testing (some performed pre-recurrence, before Oncomine DxTT approval) is a key confounder acknowledged but not addressed analytically
Generalizability limited to specialized Japanese cancer centers; selection bias from non-consecutive enrollment acknowledged but not quantified
Weak data/code availability posture: no deposited dataset or shared analytic code despite reliance on Python/lifelines pipeline
Novelty is incremental and population-specific; the parent REVEAL cohort has already reported overall biomarker testing patterns
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently conducted, STROBE-reported subgroup analysis with clinically useful real-world implementation findings but methodological limitations (immortal-time risk in OS comparison, no multiplicity correction, unaddressed timing confounder) and incremental novelty make it a strong fit for a Tier 2 oncology-focused specialty venue with minor revisions, rather than a Tier 1 practice-changing outlet.
